claims.text: At stage-2 Order.Status is a string with a private setter; the constructor sets "new", MarkPaid() "paid", Cancel() "cancelled", Ship() "shipped". The comment above MarkPaid() says no endpoint takes payments; OrderTests (unit tests of Order) calls it.
At stage-2 Order.Cancel() throws OrderStatusException only when Status is "cancelled" or "shipped"; it has no check for "paid", so a paid order becomes cancelled.

docs/team/meeting-notes-example.md (stage-2) decides a `paid` order cannot be cancelled from the app (ask for a refund), gives the reason (cancelled but money taken) and lists tasks: status check in the cancel API, hide the button, both 'this sprint'. Its only status words: `paid`, `shipped`.
docs/team/story-example.md acceptance criteria use `new` (1), `cancelled` after a customer cancels (2), `paid`/`shipped`/`cancelled` hide the button (3), and a second cancel leaves `cancelled` (5).

refund-design.md step 6 (stage-2): on gateway confirmation, in one transaction the refund row becomes `refunded` with `paid_at`, the order moves to `cancelled`, and a `pending` notifications row is added; YC-5 is a requirement in docs/team/refund-requirements.md.

refund-design.md 'Rủi ro và câu hỏi mở' (stage-2) states PATCH /api/v1/orders/{id}/cancel still cancels a `paid` order because Order.Cancel() blocks only `cancelled` and `shipped`, and leaves to the product owner whether to block it.
At stage-2 PATCH /api/v1/orders/{id}/cancel (OrdersController) leads to OrderService.CancelOrderAsync, which calls order.Cancel().
docs/team/story-example.md and meeting-notes-example.md exist from stage-0; docs/design/refund-design.md first appears at stage-2.

claims.text: Definition: a ubiquitous language is the set of words business people, documents and code use for the same things, each with one agreed meaning; it is kept in code and documents and evolves, not a one-off glossary.
claims.source_hint: DDD literature (strategic design: ubiquitous language); glossary.yaml ubiquitous-language short_en

claims.text: When a word has two business meanings or a rule exists only in a document, the team should agree a sharper word or rule with the business and change the code along with the documents; opposing view: a rename has a cost, and a team may accept a known ambiguity in a rarely queried status.
When code and a recorded business decision disagree, the disagreement is the defect and the business decides which side changes; code shows behaviour, not intent.

Business-named methods and status values (Cancel(), "cancelled") let a sentence in a document be checked by reading one method; numeric codes behind a generic setter would not (hypothetical contrast, no code shown).
